To contextualize these risks,

Chew and Cantrell $^{10}$ reviewed 1,928 tracheostomies in adults and found an overall complication rate of 15.8% and an overall mortality rate of 1.6%. By comparison, tracheostomy-related mortality in children ranges from 3.2% to 8.5%. Mortality from all causes approximates 25% but may reach 50% or more in selected groups under 1 year of age. $^{1-9}$

A recent 10-year review of pediatric tracheostomy was performed to identify trends in airway management in children and to recognize those groups of patients who are at greater risk for complication and mortality.

All tracheostomies performed in the operating room between January 1971 and December 1980 were reviewed retrospectively. A list was compiled initially from the operative log and included procedures done by otolaryngology, general surgical and cardiothoracic services. A total of 441 charts were identified and 420 were located and analyzed with respect to the following variables: age, diagnosis, indication for procedure, duration of tracheostomy, early and late complications and mortality. Early complications were defined as those occurring in the operating room or during the first postoperative week. At one week, the tracheostomy stoma has usually matured, and the first tube change is performed. Late complications were defined as those occurring after the first week.

While the absolute number of tracheostomies has remained constant each year, the incidence per hospital admission has shown a slight decrease (Table 1). There was a slight male predominance (1.4:1.0). The racial incidence appeared to reflect the racial pattern of the referral region for Children's Hospital. The age range spanned one day to 21 years; 244 patients (58%) were 2 years of age or younger; 197 (47%) were under 1 year of age. Over the 10-year period, there was a relative increase in the number of children under the age of 2 (Fig. 1).

Table 2 illustrates the distribution of primary diagnoses in patients who underwent tracheostomy. Along with CNS disorders, diseases of the upper airway were the most common primary diagnoses. Further breakdown of the upper airway obstruction category is shown in Table 3. Over the review period there was an increase in tracheostomies in elective craniofacial procedures, CNS disorders and respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and a decrease in patients with congenital heart disease (CHD).

Prolonged ventilation was the most common indication for tracheostomy in our series (53%). Other major indications included upper airway obstruction (39%) and pulmonary toilet (4%). One infant required a tracheostomy because of recurrent apnea and bradycardic episodes. Another child had bleeding of the upper aerodigestive tract which required a controlled airway. A third child could not be adequately ventilated through an endotracheal tube. An additional 4% of patients had multiple indications for tracheostomy.

Seventy-two patients (17%) were discharged directly from the hospital to home after an intensive period of training family members in tracheostomy care. Eleven patients (3%) required home ventilators for continued respiratory support. Sixty-three patients were transferred to other institutions for further care. The remaining patients were either decannulated during initial hospitalization or succumbed with an indwelling tracheostomy while still hospitalized.
With 106,298 pediatric admissions from 1971 to 1980, the average incidence in our study was 3.9 tracheostomies per 1,000 admissions.
To put this in perspective, this means that for every 1,000 children admitted to the hospital during this decade, roughly four required a surgical opening in the windpipe.
The gradual decrease over the decade (Table 1) is probably a reflection of the increasing acceptance of prolonged intubation for croup, epiglottitis and some cardiac and CNS disorders.

The higher incidence of tracheostomy in male patients has been cited by both Tucker and Silberman $^{5}$ and Oliver et al $^{1}$ and is felt to represent an increased male susceptibility to congenital and acquired disorders.
The relative increase in tracheostomy in children under 2 years of age appears to parallel the increase in survival in children with bronchopulmonary dys-

Along with CNS diseases, obstruction of the upper airway comprised the most frequent primary diagnosis. The incidence of tracheostomy in cases of upper airway obstruction, however, remained relatively constant over the 10 years of review, while CNS disorders have shown a steady increase — a reflection of prolonged survival of children with these diseases. $^{12,13}$ Elective craniofacial procedures have been performed more frequently and often require tracheostomy. $^{14}$ Prolonged ventilation has been associated with improved survival in premature infants with RDS and often necessitates tracheostomy. Only in patients with CHD has there been a substantial decline in tracheostomies, a factor which reflects changes in the philosophy of our cardiothoracic surgeons.

Over the 10-year span, both length of hospitalization and duration of tracheostomy have shown substantial increases. Again this indicates the prolonged survival of critically ill children who probably would have succumbed in the past. Children with RDS and CNS disorders frequently fall into this category. Many of these children require a tracheostomy for months for prolonged ventilation or access for pulmonary toilet.

The complication rate of 49% is similar to that reported by Tucker and Silberman $^{5}$ (46.5%) but higher than that reported by Hawkins and Williams $^{6}$ (36%), Gaudet et al $^{9}$ (33%) and Palva et al $^{8}$ (19%). Some series have included delayed decannulation as a complication. Delayed decannulation may be due to tracheostomy but is more often a result of the primary disease. This difference may be difficult to distinguish and is rarely well documented. Likewise persistent

fistula is often not included as a complication since it occurs after successful decannulation. We have

Tracheostomy in adults has generally been associated with a lower complication rate than in children. The low incidence of intraoperative complications in our series (0.5%) is most likely a result of almost all tracheostomies being performed by or under the direction of a few pediatric surgeons who are otolaryngologic, general or cardiothoracic surgeons. Almost all were performed with a controlled airway, usually an endotracheal tube. This permits a safe general anesthetic and is helpful in identifying the trachea, which tends to be less rigid in children than in adults. Meticulous attention is paid to hemostasis, and careful dissection in the midline can avoid such complications as pneumothorax. Once the trachea is identified, stay sutures are placed on either side of the midline to provide easy access to the trachea postoperatively if decannulation or tube obstruction should occur. A vertical incision through one or two tracheal rings is made between the stay sutures. In older children, particularly adolescents, an inferiorly based flap is frequently employed. After the endotracheal tube is withdrawn to a level just above the operative site, the tracheostomy is placed and secured. The skin incision is closed only partially to prevent pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema. The endotracheal tube is not completely removed until the tracheostomy tube is well secured and bilateral auscultation of the lungs reveals good breath sounds. A postoperative chest radiograph is obtained either in the operating room or in the intensive care unit. The tracheostomy tube is changed routinely at the end of the first week by a member of the operative team. The patient remains in the intensive care unit

Contrary to most other series $^{1,5,7,9}$ in which pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum were the most frequent early complications, our most common early complication was accidental decannulation followed by pneumonia. Pneumothorax is reported to occur more often in infants and younger children; our results paralleled those of Bridges et al $^{3}$ which showed a slightly higher incidence in older children. Inclusion of pneumonia as an early complication is controversial since the process may have preceded the tracheostomy. We included only those postoperative cases of pneumonia that were not clinically or radiographically evident prior to the tracheostomy as early complications.

The most frequent late complication, persistent tracheocutaneous fistula, occurred in a direct relationship to the duration of tracheostomy; approximately half of the tracheostomies of more than 1 year's duration developed a fistula (Fig. 4). Oliver et al $^{1}$ also reported a significant incidence of tracheocutaneous fistula after decannulation. Accidental decannulation was the second most common late complication and the most common overall complication. In most cases of tracheal hemorrhage, the etiology was uncertain. Several cases accompanied abnormal clotting, usually in the presence of overwhelming sepsis. In only one case was postoperative bleeding a result of operative technique, ie, a vein which required ligation. There was one occurrence of massive hemorrhage, presumably an innominate artery rupture, which resulted in the death of a patient.

As noted by Gaudet et al, $^{9}$ infants with RDS had a higher incidence of complications. Children with upper airway disease also sustained more morbidity, while there appeared to be fewer problems in cardiothoracic patients, contrary to other series. $^{9}$ The higher incidence of late complications in

When looking at the big picture of patient outcomes, our
overall mortality rate is comparable to those of other series, $^{1,6}$ while tracheostomy-related deaths are slightly fewer than most other series.
To understand why this is the case, we must look at the specific mechanisms of failure.
As noted by Tucker and Silberman, $^{5}$ accidental decannulation
(the accidental removal of the tracheostomy tube)
are the most common causes of tracheostomy-related deaths.
These events are critical because they can lead to asphyxia (suffocation) within minutes. To mitigate this risk, a significant shift in care protocols has occurred: recently,
all children, either hospitalized or at home and with critical airways, have been provided with airway occlusion or cardiac
a "smoke detector" for the airway; if the tube becomes blocked or is removed, the monitor alerts caregivers immediately, preventing
asphyxia in the event of accidental decannulation or tube obstruction.
In nontracheostomy-related deaths, mortality is a function of the severity of the underlying illness.
This means that when a child dies, it is often due to the primary disease they are fighting, rather than the tracheostomy itself.
disorders and congenital anomalies (miscellaneous disorders) demonstrated high rates
of mortality, reflecting the inherent severity of these conditions. In contrast,
craniofacial patients and those with upper airway obstruction had significantly lower
rates, suggesting that their underlying conditions, while serious, are often more manageable or less immediately life-threatening than complex cardiac or neurological failures.
Children with long-term tracheostomies, especially those associated with prolonged ventilation, present difficult management problems.
The challenge here is balancing the need for constant medical support with the desire for a normal childhood.
There are currently several children who have spent most, if not all, of their lives hospitalized for prolonged ventilation or tracheostomy care.

With intensive instruction, monitoring, and humidification and suctioning equipment, home care of children with tracheostomy can be successful. While half (four) of the tracheostomy-related deaths occurred at home and were due to accidental decannulation or tube obstruction, most occurred prior to the increased
This highlights the importance of technology in safety: as monitoring tools became more accessible, home care became safer.
Our home ventilator program has also provided an alternative to continuous hospitalization in patients who require only respiratory support. $^{15}$
In addition to the complications previously described, speech and swallowing difficulties in children with tracheostomies have also been recognized as significant long-term problems.
A tracheostomy bypasses the normal upper airway, which is crucial for producing sound and managing food.
Our experience has revealed that speech therapy is beneficial in assisting the child's normal language development. $^{16}$
communication disorders clinic has been established at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia to help monitor and treat these problems.

CONCLUSION
Pediatric tracheostomy during the past decade has been subject to changes brought on by improvements within pediatric medicine. The decrease in incidence of tracheostomy reflects an increase in the use of endotracheal intubation. The increase in duration of tracheostomy and decrease in age are a result of improvements in survival of infants with RDS

and other children with chronic and complicated primary disease. With good operative technique, operative complications can be minimal. Postoperative complications frequently mirror the complexity of the child's overall medical care. While these complications have a significant incidence, related mortality can be limited both in the hospital and at home with good training and the proper equipment, especially humidification and monitoring.
